newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Foreign buyers boost Tokyo's Nikkei, Hong Kong up.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buyers boost Tokyo's Nikkei, Hong Kong up.

text.p: Foreign investors moved back into Tokyo's share market on Thursday and their bargain-hunting pushed the key Nikkei index sharply higher, brokers said.
Hong Kong's bourse reversed two days of losses to add half a percent, but the biggest turnaround of the major Asian markets was Bombay, which jumped 2.58 percent after recent heavy falls.
Seoul lost the most ground, down 1.34 percent to close at the lowest levels in 38 months on fears of labour strife.
Bangkok's market was closed for a public holiday.
Tokyo stocks leapt more than 280 points as a rally in shares of global companies was revived, brokers said.
But some sectors were still hit by heavy sales, and overall sentiment was not completely bullish, they said.
The Nikkei 225 average surged 283.99 points, or 1.37 percent, to finish at 20,943.90.
"Blue chips such as Toyota tested new highs, and that helped to lift the market," said Akihiro Naemura, strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
Brokers said foreign investors, who had aggressively bought shares in big Japanese corporate names and had led the recent boom in blue-chip issues, started to bargain-hunt again.
"Investors, whose holdings of blue chips are still small in their portfolios, feel they don't have enough. So they rushed into buying," said a broker at a Japanese securities house.
Brokers said a power utility's performance and new evidence of a buoyant property market lifted Hong Kong stocks.
The Hang Seng index closed 57.32 points, or 0.43 percent higher at 13,491.56.

"I think Hongkong Electric is sort of leading the market," said Geoff Galbraith, institutional sales trader at Nava SC Securities. "When you are in a bull market, it is a rotational thing and we are getting back to utilities."
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange index jumped 71 points to 2815.82 after falling more than five percent in the past three sessions, traders said.
They said the market rose on a long-awaited technical recovery helped by unconfirmed newspaper reports of the government taking a more serious view of improving confidence in Indian bourses.
"It seems as if panic bells are ringing in New Delhi," said a broker who spoke anonymously. "The unabated fall in prices is making the government take note of the markets."
Jakarta's stock market touched a high for the year of 634.41 points before easing to 634.30 at the close, powered by overseas interest in banking stocks and selected blue-chips.
The Jakarta Composite Index ended up 8.03 points, or 1.28 percent, at 634.30 points.
Seoul's composite index ended 9.57 points lower at a provisional 706.30, the lowest since September 25, when it closed at 703.55.
"The escalating confrontation between labour groups and the government scares investors," said Kim Won-suk, a broker at Dongwon Securities.
Union groups object to a government labour reform plan for flexible working hours and fear worker layoffs.

The Australian share market's All Ordinaries index rose 12.6 points, or 0.53 percent, to 2,383.3, and Singapore's Straits Times Industrials Index finished 19.81 points, or 0.90 percent, higher at 2,214.17.
At 1123 GMT, the dollar traded at 112.68/2.77 yen and 1.5616/21 marks.
Gold finished lower in Hong Kong at US$368.70/369.20 an ounce against New York's $370.70/371.20 close on Wednesday.
SIMEX Brent crude futures rose late on Wednesday.
January futures last traded at $23.95 a barrel, up 17 cents from London's settlement.
